say.text: A 2-year-old with known TOF cries hard during a blood draw and turns deeply blue. The murmur you heard earlier has gone much softer.
You are alone in the OPD with no drip yet. What is your first move?

choices.label: Place the child in the knee-chest position
Give IV furosemide for the congested look
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look for the measure that needs no drug, no drip and no equipment, only the child's own body.

Intubating feels like the decisive act for a blue child. But the source describes tet spells as needing a rapid, aggressive approach built from a sequence that opens with knee-chest positioning, then oxygen.
Airway drama is not the first line; the bedside lever is.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: skipping positioning and oxygen is the classic error, because both can be done in seconds.

say.text: A blue, distressed child can look like heart failure, so a diuretic is tempting. But this is an RVOT problem: the sequence opens with positioning and oxygen, then IV fluid boluses to improve RV filling, so a diuretic points the wrong way.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a spell is not treated like heart failure.

say.text: Yes. Knee-chest positioning is the first listed measure; it increases systemic vascular resistance.
Keep that in mind. Next you will read two peers' notes, and each has one planted slip.
First, a correct write-up by Dr Rao on a similar child.  Step 1: trigger was agitation, one of the known triggers. Step 2: the murmur had softened, which fits a spell.
Step 3: knee-chest position, to increase systemic vascular resistance. Step 4: oxygen, to cause pulmonary vasodilation.
Keep this as your reference answer.

choices.label: Next, show me the peer notes

say.text: With significant RVOT obstruction most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
At rest, more obstruction gives a more prominent murmur. In a spell, little blood is crossing the narrowed outflow, so the murmur decreases in intensity.

Intern Meera's note on another spell. Step 1: murmur had gone soft, so I read it as a spell. Step 2: knee-chest, because it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance. Step 3: IV fluid bolus to improve RV filling.
One step is wrong. Which one?

choices.label: Step 1: a soft murmur cannot mean a spell
Step 3: fluids will overload this child
Step 2: the reason given for knee-chest
Compare with Dr Rao's note first

say.text: Compare each step with Dr Rao's. Two match. One names the right measure but a reason that sits on the wrong side of the circulation.
It is tempting: at rest a tighter obstruction gives a more prominent murmur. But in a spell the murmur decreases, because blood is bypassing the pulmonary bed. Step 1 is fine.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the static rule fails in a spell. Ask how much blood is crossing the outflow right now.

say.text: Fluids do sound risky if you think of heart failure. But in a spell an IV fluid bolus is given to improve RV filling, so step 3 matches Dr Rao's approach.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a spell is not heart failure, so the heart-failure reflex misleads here.

say.text: Right. The measure is correct but the stated reason is not. Now the second probe: why is that reason wrong?
Meera wrote that knee-chest works by lowering pulmonary vascular resistance. What is the correct lever?

choices.label: It increases pulmonary vascular resistance, pushing blood systemically
It reduces venous return to the right heart

say.text: Positioning does not touch the lungs' vessels. Think of the other circuit, the one the aorta feeds, and whether you want it open or tight.
You have the direction of the goal, but the lever is misplaced: knee-chest acts on the systemic side. It increases systemic vascular resistance. Pulmonary vasodilation is the job of oxygen.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: positioning is systemic resistance, oxygen is the pulmonary lever.

say.text: Reduced venous return sounds like a heart-failure measure, which makes it tempting. But the point of the sequence is the opposite: IV fluid boluses improve RV filling, and knee-chest increases systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: spells are managed by filling the RV, not unloading it.

say.text: Yes. Knee-chest increases systemic vascular resistance, as in Dr Rao's step 3. Oxygen is the one that causes pulmonary vasodilation.
It is the same balance as in pink Tets: when RVOT resistance is less than systemic resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.
Registrar Dev's note on a third spell. Step 1: knee-chest, to increase systemic vascular resistance. Step 2: oxygen. Step 3: chest looked congested, so IV furosemide and fluids held.
One step is wrong. Which?

choices.label: Step 1: positioning is not a spell measure
Step 2: oxygen should wait until drugs are given
Step 3: the diuretic and the held fluids
Compare with Dr Rao's note first

say.text: Steps 1 and 2 appear in Dr Rao's note. Look at the step that treats the child like a different condition.
Positioning looks too simple to count as treatment, which is why it is tempting to doubt. But it is the first listed measure, and it increases systemic vascular resistance. Step 1 is right.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: a simple measure is still a lever.

say.text: Drugs feel more serious than oxygen, so putting them first is tempting. But oxygen causes pulmonary vasodilation and sits right after positioning in the sequence. Step 2 is right.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: bedside measures come before the IV drugs.

say.text: Yes. That step treats the spell as heart failure. Now the second probe: what is the right way to handle volume and afterload?
Dev's step 3 is a slip. What does the spell sequence do instead?

choices.label: IV fluid bolus for RV filling; phenylephrine to raise afterload
A vasodilator to lower afterload, then digoxin
Sedate and intubate first, fluids later

say.text: Ask what each drug does to the right ventricle's filling and to the systemic resistance, rather than which one helps a failing left ventricle.
Lowering afterload is the usual heart-failure move, so it is tempting. In a spell the aim is the opposite: IV phenylephrine increases systemic afterload, and IV fluid boluses improve RV filling.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: spell drugs raise systemic resistance, they do not lower it.

say.text: Sedation and securing the airway sound safe, so this order is tempting. But the sequence opens with positioning and oxygen, and fluids come next to improve RV filling. Morphine is a sedative given during a spell, not the opener.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: bedside measures first, then fluids, then drugs.

say.text: Yes. IV fluid boluses improve RV filling, and IV phenylephrine increases systemic afterload. IV beta-blockers decrease heart rate and aid RV filling further.
Last note, from Dr Iyer. Step 1: murmur louder than ever, so spell confirmed. Step 2: knee-chest to increase systemic vascular resistance. Step 3: IV phenylephrine to increase systemic afterload.
Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 3: afterload should be lowered, not raised
Step 2: positioning acts on pulmonary resistance

say.text: Lowering afterload is the heart-failure reflex, so it is tempting. In a spell, IV phenylephrine increases systemic afterload, so step 3 is correct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the spell goal is higher systemic resistance.

say.text: This echoes the earlier slip, so it is tempting to repeat it. Knee-chest increases systemic vascular resistance; step 2 is correct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: positioning is the systemic lever.

say.text: Yes, step 1 is the planted error. Now say why a louder murmur does not fit.
Iyer's murmur reading is wrong. What does a spell actually do to the murmur, and why?

choices.label: It gets louder, since the obstruction is tighter
It softens, since blood bypasses the lungs
It stays the same; only the colour changes

say.text: It is the right rule for a stable child: the greater the obstruction, the more prominent the murmur. A spell is different: the murmur decreases in intensity.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: this is the most common slip on this topic.

say.text: A fixed murmur is plausible if you picture only the colour changing. But the intensity falls during a spell, because most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the murmur is a flow signal and flow across the RVOT falls.

say.text: Yes. During a tet spell the murmur decreases in intensity, because most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
A softening murmur in a distressed child is a warning, not an improvement.
Last one, no helper. Which pairing of measure and lever is correct?

choices.label: Knee-chest lowers PVR; oxygen raises systemic resistance
Fluids reduce venous return; phenylephrine lowers afterload
Knee-chest raises SVR; oxygen causes pulmonary vasodilation

say.text: The levers are swapped, which is easy to do. Knee-chest increases systemic vascular resistance; oxygen causes pulmonary vasodilation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: sort each measure by circuit, systemic or pulmonary.

say.text: Both read as heart-failure measures, hence the pull. In a spell, IV fluid boluses improve RV filling and phenylephrine increases systemic afterload.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: spells are not heart failure.

say.text: Yes. Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance; oxygen causes pulmonary vasodilation.
